title: India's Venture Capital Bet Shifts From Software to Rockets, Chips, and Robots
excerpt: Deep-tech startup funding in India rose 37% year-on-year even as overall venture capital declined, with Skyroot Aerospace becoming the country's first space-tech unicorn and government policy backing a long-term shift from code to hardware.
body:
• India's deep-tech startups raised 37% more year-on-year even as overall startup funding fell, with the space sector alone attracting $871 million across 285 companies
  • Skyroot Aerospace became India's first space-tech unicorn in May 2026 after a $60 million round valuing it at $1.1 billion, with Google's first backer Ram Shriram joining its board
  • The Indian government's Fund of Funds 2.0 commits Rs 10,000 crore to deep tech and advanced manufacturing with extended 20-year recognition periods for startups
  • Beyond space, Indian startups are building indigenous semiconductors, warehouse robotics, and electric air transit for global markets

A decade ago, India's venture capital playbook was straightforward: fund software engineers building consumer apps and enterprise SaaS. That script is being rewritten. Pitch decks crossing the desks of Indian investors now feature liquid-fueled rocket engines, indigenous semiconductor architectures, and electric vertical takeoff aircraft.

From Code to Orbit

The shift from bits to atoms is no longer theoretical. Skyroot Aerospace became India's first space-tech unicorn in May 2026 after raising $60 million in a round co-led by Sherpalo Ventures and Singapore sovereign wealth fund GIC, valuing the Hyderabad-based company at $1.1 billion. Ram Shriram, the American billionaire known as Google's first backer, joined Skyroot's board. Funds managed by BlackRock provided an additional $10 million in structured debt, TechCrunch reported.

Founded in 2018 by former Indian Space Research Organisation engineers Pawan Kumar Chandana and Naga Bharath Daka, Skyroot is preparing for the maiden orbital launch of its Vikram-1 rocket — which would make India only the third country after the United States and China with private orbital launch capability.

"Skyroot achieving unicorn status marks a tipping point in demonstrating that Indian space technology is a venture-scale opportunity, as opposed to only being an aspiration led by science or government."

— Kushal Bhagia, Co-founder, All In Capital

Skyroot is far from alone. The Indian space sector now counts more than 400 startups, with total investment reaching $871 million across 241 funding rounds, according to Tracxn data. Annual funding surged from $43 million in 2021 to a record $200 million in 2025. Agnikul Cosmos has built 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engines, Pixxel is deploying hyperspectral satellite constellations, and Digantara tracks orbital space debris.

Beyond Aerospace

The deep-tech wave extends well past rockets. Industrial automation companies like GreyOrange and Unbox Robotics export warehouse systems internationally. ePlane Company and Sarala Aerospace are pioneering electric air transit. Indigenous defense and semiconductor startups are designing custom silicon and ruggedized hardware to reduce dependence on foreign supply chains.

Rathnakar Samavedam, managing partner at Hyderabad Angels Fund, argues that corporate India is now a domestic growth engine for deep tech. Average corporate quarterly profits across leading sectors have surpassed Rs 10,000 crore, giving companies both the capital and mandate to invest in homegrown innovation rather than imported technology, he wrote in YourStory.

Why R&D Timelines Are Compressing

Deep-tech ventures historically required seven to ten years before reaching market commercialization. Three factors are accelerating that timeline: generative AI tools that enable faster virtual design iterations and physics simulations, cross-border supply chains that reduce prototyping costs, and startups taking an aggressive approach to securing process and utility patents early in their lifecycle.

India's deep-tech startups are also proving capital-efficient. AUM Ventures, an early Skyroot investor, launched a Rs 750 crore ($80 million) second fund in June 2026 targeting pre-seed and seed-stage deep-tech companies. The firm cited India's STEM talent pool, which develops technologies at five to ten times lower cost than global peers, Entrepreneur India reported.

Government Backing and Global Ambitions

Policy is aligning with private capital. In February 2026, the Union Cabinet approved Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0 — a Rs 10,000 crore corpus dedicated to deep tech and advanced manufacturing. The program extends recognition periods to 20 years and provides tax incentives for companies in AI, biotech, quantum computing, and advanced materials earning up to Rs 300 crore annually.

The challenges remain significant. Indian founders face intense competition from established supply chains in China and massive capital concentrations in the United States. Export controls, dual-use technology mandates, and international regulations add complexity for companies building hardware that crosses borders.

But for investors watching capital flows, the math is shifting. Deep-tech funding in India grew 37% year-on-year even as overall startup funding declined. As Samavedam argues, some of the largest venture opportunities of the coming decade may come from teams bridging the gap between software codebases and physical-world engineering — taking Indian innovation from code all the way to orbit.
nri_angle: Indian-origin venture investors and NRI engineers are increasingly backing and building deep-tech companies in India, bridging global expertise with the country's growing hardware ecosystem.
